### 2259 fix(trailers): align the trailer writer with the final-block grammar
Fixes #2256. Stacked on #2253. Merge #2253 first, then this one.

`AppendCheckpointTrailer` could write a trailer that neither `git interpret-trailers --parse` nor our own strict readers accept. `entire checkpoint attach` then printed a successful amend for linkage that did not exist.

## The mismatch

The writer and the readers disagreed about one character, leading whitespace.

`finalTrailerBlock` classifies raw lines on purpose. Git treats an indented line after a trailer as a continuation of that trailer's value, never as a new trailer. `appendTrailerLine` ran `strings.TrimSpace` before calling `IsTrailerLine`, so an indented `  Foo: bar` looked like a trailer to the writer and like body text to every reader.

A message whose final paragraph is an indented pseudo-trailer got the new trailer joined onto that paragraph with no blank line above it. The result is one paragraph that is not a trailer block, and three things follow from it:

- `attach` reported `Amended commit ... with Entire-Checkpoint: B`.
- `PostCommit` re-read the commit, found no trailer, and skipped linkage.
- `attach`'s own dedup check could not see the trailer either, so a second run appended another copy.

The commit ends up carrying trailer text that no consumer recognises, and the user is told the opposite.

## The fix

I pulled `finalTrailerBlock`'s classification loop into a shared `isTrailerBlock(lines []string) bool`, and the writer now classifies the final non-comment paragraph with it, on raw lines. One grammar, two callers. A paragraph the writer will join has to be one the readers accept.

Joining also requires a blank line between that paragraph and the content above it. That guard keeps a trailer-shaped subject line such as `fix: bug`, which `IsTrailerLine` matches for good reason, from having the trailer glued onto it. Sharing the grammar without the guard would fix the indented case and break the far more common one.

`finalTrailerBlock` behaves exactly as before. `isTrailerBlock` returns false for an empty slice, which covers the old `start == end` guard, and the old loop could only reach its final return with `seenTrailer` already true, since a non-trailer first line always hit the `default` arm.

## Scope

Whole-message occurrences stay discovery candidates, so squash resume keeps working. Only final-block placement authorizes mutation, which is the boundary #2253 sets. `ParseCheckpoint` and `ParseAllCheckpoints` are untouched.

## Verification

I proved the red state by restoring the pre-fix `trailers.go` under the new tests. Five subtests fail, and all five pass with the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestAppendCheckpointTrailerRecognizedByFinalBlockParser/indented_pseudo-trailer_paragraph
--- FAIL: TestAppendCheckpointTrailerRecognizedByFinalBlockParser/tab-indented_pseudo-trailer_paragraph
--- FAIL: TestAppendCheckpointTrailer/indented_pseudo-trailer_paragraph_starts_a_new_block
--- FAIL: TestAppendCheckpointTrailer/tab-indented_pseudo-trailer_paragraph_starts_a_new_block
--- FAIL: TestAppendCheckpointTrailer/trailer_block_ending_in_a_continuation_line_is_joined
```

`TestAppendCheckpointTrailerRecognizedByFinalBlockParser` is a writer to reader roundtrip. It asserts that every message the writer produces is one `finalTrailerBlock` reads the trailer back out of, which is the invariant that was missing rather than a restatement of the writer's own logic.

### 2254 refactor(checkpoint): use canonical Git metadata resolution (split part 2)
> **Dependency:** This PR is built on #2241 and must not merge before it. Until #2241 lands, the Files changed view includes both #2241 and this checkpoint refactor. After #2241 merges, this branch will be rebased onto `main` and force-pushed so the PR contains only the checkpoint changes.

For the checkpoint-only change before that rebase, see the [comparison against the prerequisite branch](https://github.com/MuskanPaliwal/cli/compare/refactor-git-metadata-owner...refactor-checkpoint-metadata-resolution).

Refs #2052 and #2190.

PR #2190 established the broader direction: physical Git worktree metadata should have one canonical owner instead of being rediscovered independently across the CLI. PR #2241 introduces that owner in `gitrepo` and migrates repository opening. This PR follows it by moving the checkpoint subsystem onto the canonical metadata boundary and deleting checkpoint's duplicate traversal and caching implementation.

This is intended as an ownership refactor rather than a checkpoint behavior change. Queue placement, redaction caching, persistent refs, shadow refs, locking, and caller-specific failure policies remain intact.

## Broader refactor

Checkpoint operations need to know both the current worktree root and the repository's common Git directory. The common directory determines where repository-wide state such as the push queue and redaction cache belongs, particularly when a command runs from a linked worktree.

Before this change, checkpoint resolved that metadata itself:

```text
Checkpoint operation
        │
        ▼
checkpoint.resolveGitCommonDir
        │
        ├── git rev-parse --git-common-dir
        ├── package-level mutex
        └── per-worktree cache
```

That made checkpoint a second owner of the same physical Git facts already being consolidated under `gitrepo`. It also gave checkpoint its own cache lifecycle, cancellation-dependent behavior, and subprocess cost.

After this change, checkpoint starts from the already-open repository and delegates physical metadata resolution to the canonical owner:

```text
Checkpoint operation
        │
        ▼
checkpoint.repositoryDirs
        │
        ▼
gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata
        │
        ├── Worktree root
        ├── Per-worktree Git directory
        └── Common Git directory
```

The checkpoint package retains a small adapter because checkpoint callers commonly need the worktree root and common directory together. Interpretation of `.git`, `gitdir:`, `commondir`, and linked-worktree layout remains owned exclusively by `gitrepo`.

## Why remove the checkpoint cache

The deleted cache was compensating for a Git subprocess rather than caching an expensive domain object. Once metadata resolution becomes rooted filesystem inspection, the cache no longer provides a useful ownership boundary.

Removing it has three useful consequences:

- An already-open repository no longer launches `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` when constructing checkpoint state.
- Repairs to `.git` or `commondir` metadata are observed by the next operation instead of remaining hidden behind a stale cached result.
- Checkpoint no longer owns a mutex, cache-clearing API, or cancellation-dependent cache semantics for facts owned by `gitrepo`.

This also removes the checkpoint-specific resolver and its cache-only tests.

## Checkpoint consumers moved to the canonical boundary

The migration covers the checkpoint paths that depend on repository metadata:

- rooted push-queue construction
- redaction-cache placement
- persistent ref updates
- ref-store construction
- ephemeral checkpoint storage
- shadow-ref operations
- file-lock placement

These consumers now receive metadata from the same resolver used when opening the repository, without introducing a generic Git facade or moving checkpoint-specific policy into `gitrepo`.

## Caller policy remains local

The canonical resolver reports metadata facts and errors; it does not decide whether an individual checkpoint feature is required or optional.

That distinction remains deliberate:

- Push-queue construction fails closed because enqueueing against the wrong repository directory could lose or misdirect required work.
- Redaction caching fails open because caching is an optimization and transcript redaction can continue without it.
- Persistent ref updates retain their existing locking, compare-and-swap conflict handling, retry, and cancellation behavior.
- Linked worktrees continue sharing repository-wide state through the common Git directory.
- Shadow refs and ephemeral checkpoint data retain their existing worktree-specific placement.

## Observable effect

No user-facing command or checkpoint format changes.

The operational effect is narrower:

- checkpoint metadata lookup no longer launches a Git subprocess for an already-open repository
- checkpoint metadata is no longer memoized independently from the filesystem
- malformed metadata continues to follow each caller's existing required or optional failure policy
- ordinary repositories and linked worktrees retain their existing storage locations

The checkpoint-only layer relative to #2241 contains 16 files, with 139 additions and 211 deletions. Most additions are focused behavioral tests; the production change primarily removes duplicate traversal and cache machinery.

### 2241 refactor(gitrepo): centralize metadata resolution (split part 1)
Refs #2190.

PR #2190 moved every Git metadata consumer at once. The review exposed two separate jobs: define one owner for the metadata, then migrate its callers.

This is split part 1. It adds the resolver and changes only repository opening. Checkpoint, session, strategy, hooks, and other consumers stay unchanged here.

## Files and ownership

Three production files and four test files change. All paths below are relative to `cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo/`.

| File | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `metadata.go` | No file | Resolves the three metadata facts |
| `repository.go` | Opening rediscovered paths | Resolves and passes metadata |
| `reftable.go` | Errors looked like absence | Returns inspection errors |
| `metadata_guard_test.go` | No guard | Blocks new duplicate traversal |
| `metadata_test.go` | No resolver tests | Covers real and broken layouts |
| `repository_test.go` | Tested the old path | Covers fallback and failures |
| `reftable_test.go` | Tested boolean detection | Covers inspection errors |

The call path changes like this:

```text
Before

OpenPath
  ├── resolve .git and commondir while opening
  ├── resolve them again while checking alternates
  └── fall back without one validated metadata result

After

OpenPath
  └── ResolveWorktreeMetadata
        ├── GitDir
        ├── CommonDir
        └── WorktreeID
              │
              ├── repository storage
              ├── alternates inspection
              └── reftable inspection
```

## One resolver for three facts

`gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata` resolves an explicit worktree root into:

- `GitDir`
- `CommonDir`
- `WorktreeID`

The resolver takes a worktree root. It does not discover one from CWD, read Git environment variables, run Git, cache results, or choose a caller's policy.

Resolution is all-or-error. Malformed or unreadable metadata stops the open.

`gitrepo.OpenPath` now resolves metadata once and passes those facts into repository opening, object-alternates detection, and reftable inspection.

A bare-repository open is tried only when worktree metadata does not exist.

## Symlinks and `..` keep their filesystem meaning

Lexically cleaning a path through a symlink can change where `..` leads. The resolver checks filesystem identity before it returns a cleaned path.

Linked-worktree registrations may use physical aliases. They must still resolve to an immediate child of `CommonDir/worktrees`.

Inspection errors now reach the caller. They no longer mean "feature absent." This applies to reftable inspection and malformed `.git` layouts.

## Fixes a hang that is already released

`OpenPath` on `main` identifies a `.git` entry by reading it: `os.Stat`, then `os.ReadFile`. That works for a directory or a regular file. For three other entry types the read never finishes.

| `.git` is | `main` | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A FIFO with no writer | Blocks until a writer opens it | Refused on type |
| A symlink to such a FIFO | Blocks until a writer opens it | Refused on type |
| A symlink to `/dev/zero` | Reads forever, memory grows | Refused on type |

The resolver checks the type first. It opens only a directory or a regular file, and refuses anything else by name.

None of these arrive by clone. Git refuses a `.git` path component in a tree at any depth, so each one needs local write access to the worktree. This is a robustness fix, not a vulnerability.

## `gitdir:` strictness now matches Git

The legacy parser accepted pointer files that Git rejects. It cut the prefix at `gitdir:` instead of `gitdir: `, then trimmed whitespace from the remainder. That let `gitdir:target`, ` gitdir: target`, and `gitdir:\ttarget` all resolve. Git requires the single space and trims nothing.
The fixture covers seven `.git` pointer spellings. The new resolver agrees with Git on all seven. The legacy parser agreed on three.
This changes behavior. A `.git` file that worked only because Entire was more permissive than Git now fails, and every other Git tool was already failing it.

## Stop new duplicate traversal

A source guard scans production Go across the repository. It rejects new `.git`, `gitdir:`, and `commondir` traversal outside `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata`.
The guard lists the existing callers that later PRs must migrate:

- checkpoint metadata
- session metadata
- strategy and hooks
- remaining product consumers

The exception list records each function and the one `git rev-parse` flag it may use. If that function starts using another metadata flag, the guard fails. The test also fails when a listed exception no longer exists.

A temporary multi-file repository test runs the complete scanner. It proves that the scanner follows a package constant into another file, scans production code under `internal/`, and ignores a parameter named `gitDir`.

Positive controls cover rooted filesystem APIs, package constants, `Readlink`, aliased imports, and legacy resolver calls.

  - formatting passed
  - lint passed with 0 issues
  - race-enabled unit and integration tests passed
  - Vogon canary passed 56/56
  - external deterministic canary passed 4/4

- On the seven `.git` pointer spellings in the fixture, the new resolver matches Git on 7/7. The legacy parser matched 3/7.

## Deliberately not included

### 2238 refactor(pi): remove unused active-session cache
Follow-up to #1936, which stopped a nested `pi --no-session` subagent from claiming its parent's session. That fix removed the only two readers of Pi's per-repo `pi-active-session` file and left the write/clear half for a separate change. This is that change. It deletes the cache: the writes in `session_start` and `before_agent_start`, the clear in `session_shutdown`, and the three helpers. Pi session identity now comes only from the hook payload or the session filename.

## Why the cache goes instead of staying

The single-slot `.entire/tmp/pi/pi-active-session` file cached the active session ID so a later hook arriving without one could recover it. That fallback, present since the original Pi integration (#1170), caused the bug #1936 fixed. A nested `pi --no-session` subagent auto-discovers the same project-local extension and fires hooks with no session identity. Resolving those against the per-repo slot handed the child its parent's ID, and the nested turn overwrote the parent's prompt and turn window.

The recovery it promised was never reachable either. A payload with no session file also has no transcript, so `captureTranscript` returns `""` and the event dies downstream no matter what ID the cache supplied.

The design was also wrong on its own terms. One slot per repo cannot represent two concurrent Pi sessions in the same worktree, so the second `session_start` silently overwrites the first. Deleting the store closes that tracked concern too. Hardening an identity mechanism nothing reads would have been wasted work.

## What changed

- `cacheSessionID`, `readCachedSessionID`, `clearCachedSessionID`, and the `activeSessionFile` constant are gone. `session_start` and `before_agent_start` no longer touch the filesystem, and `session_shutdown` is a pure no-op.
- `openSessionCache` loses its `create bool` parameter. `captureTranscript` is the only caller left and always creates, so the read-only `OpenAtForRead` path is gone.
- `session_shutdown` keeps its contract. It still emits no `SessionEnd`, because the extension dispatches `session_shutdown` and `agent_end` through non-blocking `execFile` and an eager `SessionEnd` would race `agent_end`'s checkpoint save. It also stays exempt from the sessionless guard, so the handler reaches its no-op deliberately instead of being skipped.
- The cache roundtrip and shutdown-clears-cache tests go away with the code. A new `TestParseHookEvent_DoesNotWriteActiveSessionCache` asserts the two formerly-writing hooks leave no `pi-active-session` behind, so reintroducing the write fails a test. The sessionless-guard test drops its cache setup and now runs parallel.
- `docs/architecture/agent-guide.md` stops documenting the file and the "removal is a follow-up" note, and describes `session_shutdown` by what it does (no `SessionEnd`) rather than by the deleted cleanup.

## Verification

- `mise run check` (fmt, lint, unit and integration tests)
- Focused Pi lifecycle and transcript-capture tests
- A real Pi 0.84.4 probe: `session_start` ran and `pi-active-session` stayed absent
- Before-and-after parser benchmarks showing the filesystem work is gone

## Deliberately unchanged

- Pi session discovery (`GetSessionDir` / `ResolveSessionFile`); the cache directory was always separate from it
- Other agents' lifecycle caches
- The `session_shutdown` hook subprocess in the TypeScript extension; it still fires, only the Go handler's side effect is gone

### 2211 fix(checkpoint): serialize OPF ref updates
Fixes #2204

A native Git checkpoint writer and an OPF rewrite could both read the same ref value and then both report a successful update. The OPF paths used go-git's compare-and-swap, which does not participate in native Git's reference-locking protocol. A native transaction could therefore commit after the OPF rewrite and silently discard it.

## The fix

Introduce `gitrepo.CompareAndSwapRef`, a shared direct-ref compare-and-swap built on a native `git update-ref --stdin` transaction. The transaction prepares the update first, acquiring Git's ref lock, verifies that the ref is not symbolic while that lock is held, and then commits.

The native helper now backs:

- shadow-branch updates
- all persistent-ref writers using `updatePersistentRef`, including the Stop hook
- both OPF rewrite paths: the shared v1 ref and per-checkpoint refs

The OPF scan remains outside the ref transaction. Its final CAS uses the value observed before the scan, so a concurrent update is rejected instead of overwritten.

`CASPersistentRef` deliberately does not acquire Entire's persistent-writer flock. Its expected value predates the call, and native Git is the correctness boundary. Avoiding the flock also prevents deadline-free pre-push operations from waiting indefinitely. Transient native lock contention is retried with a bounded budget; a genuine stale-value conflict is terminal.

## Transaction and failure behavior

The separate `git symbolic-ref` invocation is deliberate. Git does not allow `symref-verify` and an update of the same ref in one transaction because it treats them as multiple updates to that ref. Preparing the native update first keeps the ref locked while the symbolic-ref probe runs, closing the conversion race.

CAS error classification recognizes only Git's exact stale-value diagnostics. Corrupt refs, unreadable refs, namespace conflicts, and other permanent failures retain their underlying diagnosis rather than being mislabeled and retried. The v1 rewrite reports `V1RefMovedError` only after a successful reread confirms that the ref actually changed.

Cancellation closes the transaction's stdin so Git can abort cleanly. A three-second `WaitDelay` bounds shutdown if a hook or inherited pipe prevents the process from exiting.

## Performance

Routing the shared write path through the transaction increases a measured ref update from 13.4 ms to 22.0 ms—an 8.6 ms cost per update. That is under 1% of the roughly 3-second p50 Stop-hook latency.

The extra symbolic-ref process is required for the direct-ref guarantee described above; it is not an accidental round trip.

## Verification

Regression tests use real native Git transactions and cover both files and reftable repositories. They exercise:

- both OPF lost-update races
- symbolic-ref rejection and concurrent symbolic conversion
- native lock contention and bounded retry behavior
- cancellation and lock release
- malformed, corrupt, unreadable, and namespace-conflicting refs
- preservation of the original failure when a v1 ref cannot be reread

The focused race tests passed ten consecutive runs.

`mise run check` passed after the review fixes, including formatting, lint, race-enabled unit and integration tests, and the Vogon and Roger-Roger canary suites.

### 2200 fix(checkpoint): skip ref updates when a checkpoint is already migrated
Closes #2196

#1926 made persistent ref writes safe when multiple Entire processes write at once. It also moved the migration's already-imported check inside `updatePersistentRef`.

As a result, a second migration pass takes the per-ref flock and runs `git update-ref H H` for every checkpoint, even though there is nothing to update. That adds thousands of lock acquisitions and Git processes in a large repository.

### 2192 fix(setup): keep external_agents writes scoped to their settings file
Fixes #2257

Adding an external agent through the interactive management flow loaded the merged project-plus-local settings and wrote that complete object into one settings file. This could copy personal overrides into committed project configuration or turn inherited project values into stale local overrides.

## Why settings crossed scopes

`LoadEntireSettings` returns the effective runtime configuration by overlaying `.entire/settings.local.json` on `.entire/settings.json`. That merged view is correct for reads, but it no longer records which file supplied each field.

`applyAgentChanges` changed `ExternalAgents` on that merged object and then passed the whole object to either `SaveEntireSettings` or `SaveEntireSettingsLocal`. As a result, enabling one setting could also persist unrelated fields from the opposite scope and materialize default values such as `enabled: true`.

For example, a local `"log_level": "debug"` override could be copied into the committed project settings while adding an external agent with project scope.

## The fix

The agent-management path now:

1. Resolves the selected settings file with `settingsTargetFile`.
2. Reads only that file through `LoadProjectRaw` or `LoadLocalRaw`.
3. Sets only `"external_agents": true`.
4. Writes the raw object back through the matching scoped writer.

The existing `setEnabledRaw` helper was generalized to `setSettingsBoolRaw` and reused for both `enabled` and `external_agents`. Working with raw JSON preserves unrelated and unknown fields without copying values from the other settings layer or injecting typed defaults.

Malformed target settings now produce an error instead of being replaced with defaults.

## Verification

The new regression test runs the real interactive agent-management flow with a mock external agent and covers both contamination directions.

Before the fix:

```text
--- FAIL: TestManageAgents_ExternalAgentSettingDoesNotLeakAcrossScopes
    --- FAIL: .../local_settings_do_not_leak_into_project
        log_level from the opposite settings scope leaked into .entire/settings.json
    --- FAIL: .../project_settings_do_not_leak_into_local
        log_level from the opposite settings scope leaked into .entire/settings.local.json
FAIL
```

After the fix:

```text
ok  	github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli	1.616s
```

Additional checks:

- `mise run check`
- `mise run lint` — 0 issues
- Enable, disable, and external-agent scope tests:

```text
ok  	github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli	2.764s
```

## Scope

This change does not alter project/local precedence, unrelated configure behavior, or the wider settings model. It only changes how the interactive external-agent path persists `external_agents`.

### 2190 refactor(gitrepo): consolidate worktree metadata traversal
Refs #2052, particularly [the duplicate-traversal finding](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2052#issuecomment-5400538888) and [the follow-up commitment](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2052#issuecomment-5429341093).

PR #2052 exposed that several packages independently interpreted `.git`, `gitdir:`, `commondir`, and linked-worktree identity. Those implementations had already diverged on layouts such as bare containers, linked worktrees, and submodules, while session and checkpoint maintained separate caches for answers derived from the same filesystem metadata.

This consolidates those physical Git facts under the existing `gitrepo` ownership boundary and removes the duplicate traversal and cache layers.

## Why this touches 67 files

This is one ownership change with a wide dependency graph, not 67 separate features.

Before this change, checkpoint, session, strategy, settings, status, review,
investigate, trail, setup/cleanup, and Codex independently interpreted some
combination of `.git`, `gitdir:`, `commondir`, and linked-worktree identity:

```text
Before

checkpoint ─┐
session ────┤
strategy ───┤ each resolves Git metadata independently
settings ───┤ and some cache the result separately
status ─────┤
review ─────┤
Codex ──────┘

After

                    gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata
                                  │
              ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
           checkpoint          session            strategy...
```

The 67 changed files break down into 37 production files and 30 test files:

| Area | Files | Why they changed |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Canonical `gitrepo` owner | 7 | Add the resolver, repository-opening boundary, tests, and ownership guard |
| Checkpoint migration | 7 | Remove its common-directory cache and migrate consumers |
| Session migration | 7 | Remove its separate cache and preserve adoption/sweep behavior |
| Strategy and hook paths | 18 | Migrate the hottest and most policy-sensitive consumers |
| Other product consumers | 18 | Migrate settings, status, review, investigate, trail, Codex, setup, and cleanup |
| Legacy `paths` deletion | 2 | Remove the old marker-based worktree-ID parser |
| Cross-cutting proof | 8 | Update fixtures and prove caller policy and subprocess behavior |

Most production changes are small call-site migrations. The largest additions
are tests proving real Git layouts, failure behavior, ownership boundaries, and
subprocess counts. Despite the broad footprint, production Go decreases by 36
lines.

## One owner for physical worktree metadata

`gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata` now resolves one explicit worktree root into:

- its per-worktree Git directory
- its common Git directory
- its optional linked-worktree ID

The resolver has no CWD lookup, Git subprocess, cache, context, options, environment interpretation, layout taxonomy, or feature-specific policy.

Returned paths remain cleaned absolute lexical paths. Physical filesystem identity is used only to determine whether the Git directory equals the common directory and whether a linked-worktree Git directory is an immediate child of `CommonDir/worktrees`.

- the checkpoint common-directory cache
- duplicate `.git` and `commondir` traversal

- the old `paths` worktree metadata helpers
- migration wrappers that would otherwise preserve fragmented ownership

A source guard rejects new production parsing of `gitdir:`, `commondir`, or independent `.git` filesystem traversal outside `gitrepo`, with two documented policy-only exceptions.

### 2188 fix(strategy): bound turn checkpoint finalization
Closes #2148

Turn checkpoint finalization can update several provisional checkpoints during an agent's TurnEnd or Stop hook. Before this change, each remote ref and blob fetch had its own time limit, but `finalizeAllTurnCheckpoints` had no deadline for the complete batch.

A slow-but-responsive remote could let every fetch finish just under its individual limit. Those requests would never trigger the existing dead-network memos, while their accumulated latency could still exceed the host's hook timeout. The host could then kill Entire before state persistence and cleanup completed, leaving checkpoints with provisional mid-turn transcripts and only warning logs to explain what happened.

## Why the existing fetch guards were not enough

The ref-fetch and blob-fetch failure memos prevent a completely unavailable remote from consuming the same fetch budget once per checkpoint. They deliberately do not memoize successful but slow requests.

Finalization loops over every checkpoint created during the turn, and one checkpoint can require multiple missing blobs. Its worst-case duration therefore grows with both the checkpoint count and the number of remote objects needed. The safety boundary has to enclose the complete finalization pass, not just each network operation.

## The fix

`finalizeAllTurnCheckpoints` now creates one deadline context for the complete pass and carries it through checkpoint-store access and writes. It also checks the deadline before starting another checkpoint.

The budget is selected by agent:

- Codex and Claude Code receive 20 seconds because their TurnEnd hooks have verified headroom.
- Pi and all other or unknown agents receive five seconds. This fits within Pi's 10-second subprocess limit and gives future integrations a conservative default.

If the deadline expires during a checkpoint write, the active operation is cancelled and no additional checkpoint fetch begins. The current and remaining checkpoints count as finalization errors, `CaptureDegradedAt` is recorded, and control returns so normal turn cleanup can continue.

Checkpoints finalized before the deadline keep their completed transcripts. Unfinished checkpoints retain their provisional transcripts. Pending checkpoint IDs are cleared according to the existing best-effort contract; this change does not introduce a durable retry queue.

`entire status` now describes `CaptureDegradedAt` generically because it can represent either a status scan or checkpoint finalization exceeding its capture budget.

### 2131 perf(checkpoint): batch persistent session writes with CAS
## Problem

`process_sessions` still persists each session separately. For every session, it reloads the checkpoint, rebuilds the session index and summary, creates a commit, and advances the checkpoint ref.

Issue #2091 measures that work at roughly 73–103 ms per session. The repeated checkpoint load and rebuild make condensation slower as more sessions share a checkpoint.

Checkpoint-level batching needs two things first:

- Ref updates must detect concurrent writes from hooks, worktrees, CLI processes, and other Git clients.
- Both persistent Git layouts must use the same batch algorithm.

## Solution

This PR adds native compare-and-swap publication and a shared `BatchSessions` write request.

It lays the storage and concurrency groundwork for #2091 item 2. It does not yet change PostCommit to group and submit sessions in batches. That work is listed below.

## Native compare-and-swap publication

`CompareAndSwapRef` publishes refs through native Git:

```text
git update-ref <ref> <new> <expected-old>
```

Missing-ref creation passes the correct all-zero object ID in both SHA-1 and SHA-256 repositories.

`RunRefTransaction` retries a logical mutation when another writer wins the race. Each attempt reads the current tip, rebuilds from that tip, and publishes with CAS. Conflicts use bounded, cancellation-aware jitter. The transaction stops after 16 attempts.

A mutation that reports `changed=false` is an idempotent no-op and does not call `git update-ref`.

The CAS conversion covers persistent v1 metadata refs and per-checkpoint refs, including:

- initial ref creation;
- v1 migration;
- attribution, summary, and transcript backfills;
- reconciliation and safe local ref advancement;
- orphan cleanup and expected-old deletion;
- shadow-branch migration;
- rewind publication;
- OPF publication.

OPF uses one CAS attempt by design. If its expected ref has moved, it fails closed and withholds the push. It does not rebuild sanitized output from newly appeared content.

Go-git object construction now takes a process-local lock keyed by `*git.Repository`. This protects go-git state shared by concurrent writers in one process. Native Git CAS handles publication conflicts between processes.

## Checkpoint-level batch writes

`BatchSessions` is now part of the sealed `WriteRequest` union. One request contains a checkpoint ID and one or more reserved session writes.

Validation happens before object construction:

- The checkpoint ID must be present and valid.
- Every session must reference that checkpoint.
- Session IDs must be valid and unique.
- Sessions are sorted by `SessionID`.
- Task tool-use IDs and agent IDs must be valid.
- Duplicate task IDs within or across incoming sessions are rejected.
- Sessions without timestamps share one UTC timestamp, truncated to seconds.
- Author fallback, commit-message inputs, and prepared tree hashes are fixed before CAS retries.

`GitStore` and `gitRefsStore` share the same preparation and checkpoint-tree builder. Their wrappers only locate or splice the checkpoint subtree and choose the ref to publish.

For each CAS attempt, the builder:

- loads the existing checkpoint once;
- reads each existing session’s metadata once;
- reuses the numeric index when updating a session;
- preserves untouched session subtree hashes;
- appends new sessions in canonical order;
- merges the task subtree once and preserves untouched tasks;
- reduces the complete final session set into the root summary;
- preserves combined attribution and sticky review, investigation, and import flags;
- aggregates counts, tokens, files, strategy, branch, and commit SHA deterministically;
- creates one checkpoint commit for that backend attempt.

Existing `Session` and `ReservedSession` requests pass through the same builder with one session. Their caller contract does not change.

Combined attribution stays in its existing backfill transaction. The batch write does not fold it into the checkpoint commit.

## Storage and compatibility

The durable checkpoint format does not change:

```text
metadata.json
0/metadata.json
0/full.jsonl
0/transcript.jsonl
1/...
tasks/<tool-use-id>/...
```

Older clients already understand checkpoints with multiple numbered session directories. A batch produces the same tree, task subtree, summary, and metadata types that repeated single-session writes produce.

Compatibility was checked in separate dimensions:

- New clients continue to read existing checkpoint data.
- Old clients can read checkpoints written by `BatchSessions`.
- Existing callers still use `Writer.Write(context.Context, WriteRequest)`.
- Single-session requests keep their existing behavior.
- Malformed or ambiguous requests now fail before publication.
- Concurrent upgraded writers protect each other with native CAS.
- If an old blind writer publishes first, the CAS writer detects the change and rebuilds.
- If an old blind writer publishes second, it can still overwrite the newer write. One upgraded participant cannot make a pre-CAS writer safe.

Rejecting invalid input and replacing last-writer-wins behavior with conflict detection are intentional safety changes, not storage incompatibilities.

## Routing and partial success

Persistent dispatch, kind routing, fanout, and the filesystem test store support `BatchSessions`.

One Git backend makes every session in the batch visible through one ref update. Fanout writes the primary first. Mirror failures remain logged and best-effort, so they do not turn a successful primary write into an error.

Routing follows the backend encoded by the checkpoint ID if configuration changes after reservation. If a readable migrated copy exists, routing updates that copy too. The read-preferred backend is probed before the first physical write.

There is no transaction across physical backends. If the second backend fails, the first may already contain the batch. The writer returns the error. Retrying the same canonical upsert repairs the lagging copy.

A future lifecycle caller must therefore treat an error as “some backend may already contain this batch,” not as proof that nothing was written.

The filesystem store replaces one JSON document atomically under a process-local mutex. It is a test backend and does not provide cross-process serialization.

## Complexity

The deterministic visitation test uses existing checkpoints with 100, 200, and 500 sessions. With no tasks, it records:

```text
root entries visited          N + 1
session entries visited       N
existing metadata reads       N
task entries visited          0
final-session contributions   N
total                         4N + 1
```

These counters measure visits to checkpoint content, not every CPU operation.

One CAS attempt against one Git backend performs one checkpoint load and build. It does not rescan the checkpoint for each incoming session. Request preparation happens once before the retry loop. A CAS conflict causes one more load and build from the winning tip.

## Validation

`mise run check` passed on the committed tree. This included:

- formatting;
- golangci-lint with zero issues;
- the aggregate race-enabled unit and integration suite;
- Vogon, 56 of 56;
- roger-roger, 4 of 4.

Focused race-enabled tests also passed for:

- batch validation, ordering, summaries, timestamps, trailers, task collisions, and both Git layouts;
- concurrent metadata-ref and per-checkpoint-ref writes;
- SHA-1 and SHA-256 CAS;
- transaction retries and cancellation;
- initialization and migration;
- dispatch, kind routing, fanout, and filesystem storage;
- reconciliation, cleanup, ref advancement, rewind, and OPF publication;
- persistent-ref writer coverage.

The advisory duplication scan found nothing in `persistent_batch.go`. Its production persistent-backend findings come from older read-wrapper patterns. The only related new finding is duplicated routing-test setup.

No paid real-agent E2E tests were run.

## Left for the next PR

PostCommit still writes sessions one at a time. Completing #2091 item 2 requires the lifecycle layer to:

1. Group materialized `process_sessions` results by checkpoint ID.
2. Build one `BatchSessions` request per checkpoint.
3. Persist enough intent to recover after a process crash.
4. Submit one batch write per checkpoint.
5. Retry safely when one physical backend may already contain the batch.
6. Keep combined attribution as a separate transaction.
7. Remove completed intent only after every required primary write succeeds.
8. Define when stale intent can be removed without losing recoverable work.
9. Test interruption before publication, partial backend success, retry, and cleanup.
10. Re-run the commit-hook performance tests and confirm that checkpoint loading and building happen once per checkpoint.

Until that work lands, single-session writes are safer and use the shared builder, but the full `process_sessions` latency reduction is not active.

Task-v2 storage, attribution folding, unrelated CLI cleanup, and the existing commit-hook performance-test work remain out of scope.

## Review status

Stages 1 and 2 were reviewed independently. No Critical, High, or Medium correctness defect was found.

The remaining hardening ideas are non-blocking:

- Check cancellation again after acquiring the repository object lock.
- Replace the lexical persistent-ref writer inventory with an AST-based check.
- Narrow native Git’s `cannot lock ref` error classification if callers need more precise operational errors.
- Revisit process-lifetime lock-map retention if this code moves into a long-running process that repeatedly opens repositories.

### 2099 fix(claude-code): capture Stop transcripts as validated snapshots
Refs #2091, item 3 only.

Before this change, Claude Code's Stop hook waited for a transcript sentinel that no longer appears, then fell back to a 500 ms quiet window. The wait only validated a mutable path. Lifecycle copied that path later, and provisional-checkpoint finalization opened it once more. Entire could therefore store bytes other than the ones it had treated as ready.

This PR replaces that sequence with one owned, validated snapshot for Claude Stop. Modern Claude payloads provide the final assistant response, so Entire can validate a transcript immediately with no artificial wait. Older payloads retain the 500 ms quiet-window fallback. The lifecycle also keeps checkpoints refreshable across Claude's repeatable Stop events and derives file and token metadata from one transcript parse.

## The wait did not own the transcript

TranscriptPreparer returns only an error. It gives the caller no bytes, open handle, identity, size, or file version. A successful wait says that path state A looked ready, but lifecycle can then copy state B and checkpoint finalization can read state C.

Shortening the wait alone would reduce latency while leaving that race intact. Valid final JSON would not be enough either: a complete older prefix can be syntactically valid even when the current turn has not reached the file.

## Owned, validated Stop snapshots

The built-in Claude Code adapter now has a Stop-specific capture operation. It:

1. fingerprints the producer-owned transcript by file identity, size, and modification time;
2. reads exactly the observed byte range;
3. verifies both the opened handle and current path still identify the observed file version;
4. validates the JSONL and derives the position from those exact bytes; and
5. returns an Entire-owned snapshot used by lifecycle, metadata analysis, position advancement, and checkpoint finalization.

None of those consumers reopens Claude's live transcript for the same Stop. If the file changes during capture, the bytes are discarded and capture retries against the new version.

The portable fingerprint catches ordinary appends, truncation, replacement, and rewrites whose modification time changes. It cannot prove that a same-size rewrite did not happen when the filesystem also reports the same timestamp. Claude appends transcript records, so that is an acceptable limit here; the tests do not claim stronger detection.

## Modern readiness is evidence-based and immediate

For modern payloads, non-empty last_assistant_message supplies current-turn evidence. Capture requires a transcript position successfully measured at TurnStart, reconstructs the latest assistant text only after that boundary, and requires it to match Claude's supplied final response.

The first readiness check now runs immediately. The previous design waited for the first 50 ms ticker event even when the transcript was already complete. After the immediate attempt, incomplete captures return to the normal 50 ms polling cadence.

A rejected file fingerprint is remembered. Entire does not reread and revalidate the same unchanged 70 MiB snapshot every 50 ms; it waits until file identity, size, or modification time provides new evidence.

Missing, stale, incomplete, continuously changing, mismatched, timed-out, and canceled captures return no snapshot. The maximum wait remains three seconds.

## Legacy payloads keep the quiet-window fallback

When last_assistant_message is missing, null, or empty, Entire has no producer evidence that the current final response reached the transcript. It therefore retains the 500 ms quiet window used by older Claude Code versions.

The split is intentional:

| Payload | Readiness evidence | Timing behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Modern | Stable owned snapshot, valid current-turn JSONL, final response match | Immediate first check; 50 ms polling only when not ready |
| Legacy | Stable owned snapshot, structurally valid ending, 500 ms without file changes | Always pays the quiet window |

## Repeatable Claude Stops remain refreshable

A blocking Claude Stop hook can cause the same assistant turn to continue and later emit another Stop without a new UserPromptSubmit event. A valid last_assistant_message proves readiness for one Stop; it does not prove that Claude will never continue afterward.

Claude therefore advertises a repeatable turn-end capability. After each Stop, Entire:

- finalizes checkpoints using the validated snapshot available at that Stop;
- retains the original turn boundary and checkpoint IDs;
- tracks commits made during a continuation; and
- refreshes the same checkpoints if another Stop arrives.

The next user prompt or SessionEnd seals the turn. stop_hook_active is preserved as protocol metadata but is not treated as proof that a Stop is permanently final.

If the latest checkpoint refresh fails, Entire keeps the last successfully stored transcript and preserves the checkpoint IDs as recovery bookkeeping. Successful session-end refreshes release those IDs; failed ones keep the supporting shadow-branch state protected from cleanup.

## File and token analysis share one parse

Claude file extraction and token calculation previously implemented separate capabilities, each of which parsed the same main transcript and subagent transcripts independently.

The optional TranscriptTurnAnalyzer capability now parses the current main turn once and derives both modified files and token usage from those records. Each subagent transcript is likewise parsed once for both results. Other agents retain the existing independent capability fallback.

Capture validation remains a separate, lightweight safety pass. Its question is whether the bytes are safe and complete; turn analysis answers what metadata those validated bytes contain.

## Capture and analysis timing

These are medians from three runs on an Apple M3. They measure transcript capture, validation, and transcript-backed metadata analysis, not complete end-to-end Stop-hook latency.

### Modern Claude Stop hook

| Transcript case | Capture + validation | File/token analysis | Total transcript latency |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 KiB normal turn | 0.170 ms | 0.249 ms | 0.419 ms |
| 4 MiB large turn | 8.848 ms | 15.966 ms | 24.814 ms |
| 70 MiB session, small current turn at tail | 13.134 ms | 19.308 ms | 32.442 ms |
| 70 MiB entirely belonging to current turn | 152.057 ms | 281.803 ms | 433.860 ms |

The realistic large-history case is the third row: the transcript file is 70 MiB, but most records belong to earlier turns. The 433.860 ms case deliberately makes all 70 MiB one enormous current turn.

### Legacy Claude Stop hook

| Transcript case | Capture including quiet window | Analysis | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 KiB | 501.098 ms | 0.249 ms | 501.347 ms |

| 70 MiB session, small tail turn | 514.228 ms | 19.308 ms | 533.536 ms |

Other timing cases:

- A modern transcript that is already ready has no artificial wait.
- If writing finishes after Stop begins, latency is the remaining write delay plus approximately 50–100 ms stability detection and processing time.
- A transcript that never becomes valid, or whose final response never matches, times out after three seconds.
- Missing or already stale transcripts fail immediately.

The common modern case moves from the previous PR design's unavoidable 50 ms first poll to actual processing time: under 1 ms for a small transcript and about 32 ms for a realistic 70 MiB historical session.

Focused tests cover:

### 2053 refactor(`jsonutil`): centralize streaming atomic replacement
Depends on #1877. Until that PR merges, review the stacked range `3a39273b..7c62491a5`.

This change moves OpenCode’s staged transcript publication into `jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicStream`. The previous implementation kept temporary-file creation, validation, rename retries, and recovery inside OpenCode even though most of that lifecycle is general atomic-write behavior. The shared implementation keeps publication ordered as produce, sync, close, validate, chmod, rename, and best-effort directory sync.

## Core Changes

`WriteFileAtomicStream` now owns the staging file from creation through publication. Producer and validator errors are returned unchanged. Any failure before publication leaves the existing destination untouched and makes a best-effort attempt to remove the staging file. If a completed and validated file cannot be renamed into place, the helper returns a `PublishError` and transfers ownership of the retained staging path to the caller so the output can be recovered.

Windows replacement contention is handled inside `jsonutil` rather than OpenCode. Only access-denied and sharing-violation failures are retried, with five total attempts and cancellation-aware waits. The follow-up review found a cancellation window between retries: cancellation could occur after a wait, but the next rename could still replace the destination. The retry loop now checks the context before every rename attempt, retaining the validated staging file if cancellation wins.

OpenCode continues to translate publication failures into its existing actionable “export saved at …” message. Its package-specific staging, rename, and contention helpers have been removed because those responsibilities now belong to the shared atomic-write implementation.

## API Notes

This adds the public `jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicStream` helper and the public `jsonutil.PublishError` ownership contract. A caller receiving `PublishError` owns the validated file at `StagedPath` and must either recover or remove it.

The existing `jsonutil.WriteFileAtomic` function uses the same private engine but keeps its previous behavior. Rename failures do not expose `PublishError`, and its staging files are still cleaned up instead of being retained.

## Compatibility / Release Notes

OpenCode command invocation, timeout and error classification, mock export mode, transcript validation, attach behavior, transcript protocol, and declared capabilities are unchanged. Failed, partial, empty, invalid, and cancelled exports cannot replace an existing valid transcript.

No unrelated temporary-file or rename-based writers are migrated in this change because they may have different locking, permission, confinement, executable, or cross-filesystem requirements.

### 2052 fix(codex): use repository hook root in linked worktrees
Fixes #2020.

Codex 0.149.0 can load project hooks from a different checkout than the one in which it is running. In a conventional linked worktree, its app-server `hooks/list` response reports the primary checkout's `.codex/hooks.json`; a divergent file present only in the linked worktree is not loaded.

This PR makes that effective location visible without giving Entire ownership of another checkout. Discovery and mutation are deliberately separate: Entire may inspect the file Codex actually loads, but installs, removes, and cleans hooks only in the exact checkout where the command was invoked.

## Discovery and ownership

- `WorktreeHooksPath` identifies `<current-checkout>/.codex/hooks.json`. It is the only mutation target used by install, uninstall, presence, freshness, deselection, and clean flows.
- `DiscoveredHooksPath` identifies the project hooks file Codex is expected to load. It is used only for read-only configuration and trust diagnostics.
- `ResolveHookDiscovery` consumes the shared `gitrepo.ResolveGitLayout` classification rather than maintaining a Codex-specific `.git`, `commondir`, or worktree-marker parser.
- Conventional linked worktrees discover the primary checkout's hook file. Normal checkouts, ordinary submodules, and separate-Git-directory checkouts discover their own hook file.
- `.bare/worktrees`, linked submodules, contradictory metadata, and other behavior not pinned against Codex are reported as unresolved. Entire does not claim an unsupported layout or guess a writable fallback.

`HookDiscovery` carries no write target, migration path, cleanup path, or lock path. Its `RepositoryWide` bit describes the reach of the configuration Codex discovers; it does not authorize repository-wide mutation.

## Checkout-local mutation

`entire enable`, `entire agent remove codex`, agent deselection, and `entire clean` mutate only the current checkout's `.codex/hooks.json`. They do not create another checkout's `.codex` directory, migrate a worktree-local file into the primary checkout, remove a discovered file owned elsewhere, or perform repository-wide cleanup.

Concurrent updates are serialized only with `<current-checkout>/.codex/hooks.json.lock`. There is no `entire-codex-hooks.lock` in the Git common directory and no synchronization across worktrees. An old common-directory lock, if present from a previous build, is neither used nor cleaned from another checkout.

Current-checkout writes are hardened before the final atomic replacement:

- the logical target must be exactly `<current-checkout>/.codex/hooks.json`;
- redirected `.codex` directories, final-file symlinks, non-regular files, unrelated destinations, and Git-metadata redirection are rejected;
- existing user hooks, unknown hook events, and unrelated top-level fields are preserved;
- uninstall removes only Entire-managed entries;
- an existing file keeps its permission bits, while a new file uses `0600`.

## Bounded read-only inspection

The local and discovered files are inspected independently as absent, user-only, Entire-managed, invalid, or unresolved. Inspection is contained to the exact canonical `.codex` directory, requires a stable regular file, caps `hooks.json` at 1 MiB, reads through a limit with one overflow byte, and checks file identity before and after the read. It never creates a directory, rewrites configuration, removes entries, or acquires a mutation lock.

The structured inspection also reports whether the core Entire events are present, which current events are missing, whether managed commands and timeouts match this CLI, whether the current checkout has the project layer Codex requires, whether local trust records were readable, and which declared hooks lack an approval record. Entire does not compute, copy, or synthesize Codex trust hashes.

## Diagnostics and remedy

- `entire doctor` reports the current-worktree path and Codex-discovered path, invalid or unresolved discovery, a missing project layer, managed hook drift, and trust gaps.
- `entire status` keeps current-checkout installation/freshness semantics separate from effective Codex discovery and exposes the mismatch under the existing `codex_hooks` JSON object without changing the warning wording established in this PR.
- SessionStart appends a short, bounded, read-only discovery or trust warning when applicable.

When hooks exist only in a linked worktree, Entire does not repair the primary checkout automatically. The user-owned remedy is to commit `.codex/hooks.json` and apply that commit to the primary checkout (typically by cherry-pick), or run `entire enable` from the primary checkout. Because linked worktrees share Git objects, the commit is immediately available to cherry-pick; no push or fetch is required.

## Pinned Codex integration contract

`TestCodexAppServerHooksList_LinkedWorktreeUsesPrimaryCheckout` is a no-model integration test pinned to `@openai/codex@0.149.0`. It:

1. creates a normal repository and conventional linked worktree with distinct hook markers;
2. starts `codex app-server` in the linked worktree with an isolated `CODEX_HOME`;
3. sends `initialize`, `initialized`, and `hooks/list` JSONL messages over stdio;
4. requires the primary marker and primary `sourcePath`;
5. rejects the linked-only marker; and
6. requires empty `warnings` and `errors`.

The test makes no model request and needs no OpenAI credentials. Local integration runs skip when the exact Codex binary is unavailable. CI installs version 0.149.0 and sets `ENTIRE_TEST_REQUIRE_CODEX_APP_SERVER=1`, so a missing binary or version drift fails rather than silently skipping.

## Verification status

The implementation includes focused unit coverage for Git-layout classification, path-role separation, current-checkout-only install/remove/clean behavior, exact-worktree locking, destination containment, symlink refusal, bounded reads, mode preservation, doctor/status/SessionStart diagnostics, trust inspection, and JSON output, plus the pinned app-server integration contract above.

Full formatting, lint, unit, integration, canary, duplication, and `mise run check` verification is intentionally deferred to implementation-order item 9.

### 2038 fix(strategy): prevent duplicate session-end checkpoints
Fixes #2035.

Session-end condensation could make a checkpoint durable before its updated session state was saved. If the hook was killed in that window, recovery still considered the transcript unfinished and could write it again under a different checkpoint ID.

On current `main`, the immediate `PostCommit` path described in the issue no longer reproduces this for a no-files session because that path discards it. The durable failure still reproduces through `entire doctor`, which sees the ended session as unfinished and previously generated a new checkpoint ID for the same transcript range.

### Approach

This PR uses a write-ahead checkpoint ID. It saves the intended ID as `CondensationAttemptID`, writes the checkpoint with that ID, advances the session bookkeeping, and then clears the pending attempt. If the process dies after the write, the next attempt reuses the same ID instead of creating a duplicate.

The reservation is also honored during commit preparation and `PostCommit`. If `PostCommit` receives a different checkpoint ID, it preserves the interrupted session and shadow branch rather than overwriting its recovery state.

Advancing `LastCheckpointID` or `CheckpointTranscriptStart` before writing would prevent duplication but introduce a data-loss window: state could claim that a transcript was saved when the checkpoint write had failed. The pending ID records durable intent without claiming that the write succeeded.

`CondensationRecoveryPending` separately records when recovery may need to reconcile an interrupted write created by an older CLI version. This keeps the more expensive storage lookup out of normal condensation paths.

Reserved writes are routed using their checkpoint ID format. If checkpoint configuration changes between reservation and retry, the checkpoint is still written to the backend that originally generated its ID.

### Recovering state from older CLI versions

Older interrupted sessions have no pending checkpoint ID. Doctor reconciles them using the session identity, transcript bounds and content, checkpoint counts, agent and turn metadata, touched files, and session kind. Externalized images are reinserted before comparing transcripts.

Storage listing or reading failures stop recovery and preserve its state for another retry rather than being treated as “checkpoint not found.” If the session has genuinely advanced, recovery creates a new checkpoint instead of reusing the older one.

### Related findings

`checkpoint list` exposes both duplicates because they have different checkpoint IDs, while `tokens profile` can count both and inflate checkpoint-observed token totals. The latter already warns about overlapping checkpoint history.

Codex kills timed-out hook process groups with `SIGKILL`, not `SIGTERM`, so Entire cannot print its normal termination message during a Codex timeout. See Codex’s [hook runner](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/bb701f1e8c8db884fa0cdafff4b8dcb1604f2fdd/codex-rs/hooks/src/engine/command_runner.rs) and [process-group cleanup](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/bb701f1e8c8db884fa0cdafff4b8dcb1604f2fdd/codex-rs/utils/pty/src/process_group.rs).

### Follow-up plan

This PR lands the non-destructive part first: it prevents new duplicate checkpoints, makes retries deterministic, and reconciles interrupted writes from older CLI versions. It deliberately does not remove or hide duplicate pairs that already exist.

Questions for a follow-up:

1. Should existing duplicate pairs remain as physical history and be collapsed only in `checkpoint list` and `tokens profile`, or should `doctor` repair the stored history?
2. If one checkpoint becomes canonical, which should win: the original session-end write or the later recovery write? What should happen when their metadata differs?
3. Should repair be automatic, an explicit doctor action, or reporting-only until the user chooses?
4. Should transcript-range idempotency become a shared rule for every condensation entry point, or remain limited to session-end and doctor recovery?

Once those product choices are clear, existing duplicates can be handled separately without coupling destructive cleanup or changed read semantics to this durability fix.

### Verification

Regression coverage includes pending ID reuse, legacy orphan reconciliation, repeated storage read failures, recovery-marker persistence, mismatched commit IDs, backend changes between reservation and retry, and advanced sessions receiving a genuinely new checkpoint.

`api/checkpoint.WriteRequest` adds `ReservedSession` for writes whose checkpoint ID was previously persisted. Session state adds the optional `CondensationAttemptID` and `CondensationRecoveryPending` fields.

### Compatibility / Release Notes

Existing session-state files remain compatible because the new fields are optional. Existing duplicate checkpoints are not removed, hidden, or rewritten, and `checkpoint list` and `tokens profile` behavior is unchanged.

This does not add global transcript-range deduplication or storage scans to normal checkpoint writes. Normal writes still use the configured primary and mirrors; ID-based backend routing applies only to reserved retries.

### 2027 fix(opencode): preserve prompts after metadata fallback
Fixes #2001.

## Problem
OpenCode emits a user `message.updated` event before the `message.part.updated` event containing the prompt text. The plugin starts the turn from that metadata event with an empty prompt so a fast agent commit still sees an ACTIVE session. Because the message was then marked as seen, the later text part was ignored and checkpoints lost the user prompt.

The first version of this PR kept a marker for those promptless starts and fired `turn-start` again when the text arrived. That recovered the prompt, but `turn-start` is not a prompt setter. It captures pre-prompt Git state, creates a new `TurnID`, recalculates prompt attribution, and clears `LastCheckpointID` and `TurnCheckpointIDs`.

The timing this fallback exists for makes that destructive. A checkpoint may already have been created between the empty metadata event and the text event.

The new integration regression exercises exactly that order:

```
message.updated
  → turn-start with empty prompt
  → agent commit and checkpoint
  → message.part.updated with prompt text
```

Against the second-`turn-start` implementation, the prompt was recorded, but the original turn ID changed, the pre-prompt snapshot was replaced, attribution was recalculated, and both checkpoint fields were cleared.

## Fix
Keep the early empty `turn-start`, but repair the missing text through a new internal `PromptUpdate` lifecycle event.

`PromptUpdate` writes the late text to `prompt.txt` and updates session `LastPrompt`. It does not call `CapturePrePromptState` or `InitializeSession`, so it cannot start another logical turn or reset checkpoint bookkeeping.
The file and state updates run inside `MutateSessionState`. Checkpoint condensation clears `prompt.txt` while holding the same session lock, so either ordering is safe:

- If repair gets the lock first, condensation sees and checkpoints the prompt before clearing the file.
- If condensation gets the lock first, repair writes the prompt after condensation finishes, leaving it available for turn-end finalization.
The OpenCode plugin keeps a `promptlessTurnStarts` marker per message. Empty text updates leave the marker pending; the first non-empty part sends one synchronous `prompt-update`; later duplicates do nothing. Multiple pending messages are tracked independently. The set is cleared on session switches, session deletion, and server disposal.

The generated plugin template and the checked-in dogfood plugin remain byte-identical.

## Cost
The plugin does expected `O(1)` set work per event and keeps `O(P)` additional state for `P` promptless messages awaiting text.
A late repair starts one synchronous hook subprocess, reads and rewrites `prompt.txt` in `O(Q + L)` time for existing prompt data `Q` and incoming prompt length `L`, and performs `O(S)` session-state I/O for state size `S`.

It performs no worktree scan. The earlier second-`turn-start` path repeated work proportional to worktree size `F`, including both status walks used by turn initialization.

In the real OpenCode run, the empty `turn-start` took 74 ms and the subsequent `prompt-update` took 5 ms in the same repository.

## Verification

- [x] Regression test fails before the fix by capturing only the empty fallback prompt.
- [x] Regression test passes after the fix with `turn-start("")` followed by `prompt-update("preserve this prompt")`.
- [x] Duplicate text-part updates do not trigger additional hooks.
- [x] OpenCode package tests pass.
- [x] `mise run check` passes, including lint, race-enabled unit and integration tests, and E2E canary tests.
- [x] The generated plugin template matches the repository’s installed OpenCode plugin.
- [x] A real `opencode run` session produced a checkpoint containing the complete original prompt.
- [x] A checkpoint occurring between the metadata event and prompt-text event preserves the original turn and checkpoint bookkeeping.
- [x] Prompt repair avoids repeating the complete `turn-start` lifecycle.

## Scope
`PromptUpdate` is an internal lifecycle event used only by OpenCode in this change. There are no new CLI flags, settings, dependencies, or changes to other agent integrations.

### 1996 fix(opencode): report transcript export failures during attach
Stacked on #1877. Refs #1876.

## Problem

#1877 lets `entire session attach <session-id> --agent opencode` run `opencode export` when Entire does not already have the transcript. If that export fails, the error is written only to debug logs. Attach continues through its fallback paths and can eventually report:

```text
transcript not found for agent "opencode" with session ses_missing; is the session ID correct?
```

That message loses the real failure. A missing OpenCode executable, a timeout, invalid JSON, insufficient permissions, and an OpenCode rejection can all look like an incorrect session ID.

## Change

The attach resolver now remembers an error returned by `TranscriptFetcher` while it tries the existing project-directory fallback. If the fallback finds a transcript, attach succeeds and the fetch error is ignored. If the fallback also fails, attach returns the fetch error instead of replacing it with the generic transcript-not-found message.

The resolver remains agent-agnostic. It does not inspect OpenCode errors or branch on the agent name. Each `TranscriptFetcher` owns the errors produced by its fetch mechanism. OpenCode is currently the only implementation, so its export runner now translates the common failures:

| Failure | Terminal message |
| --- | --- |
| OpenCode is missing | `OpenCode is not installed or is not available in PATH.` |
| Export times out | `OpenCode export timed out after 30s. Try again.` |
| OpenCode rejects the export | `OpenCode could not export session "ses_123": <OpenCode error>` |
| OpenCode cannot be executed | `OpenCode could not be started because of insufficient permissions.` |
| Export contains invalid JSON | `OpenCode returned invalid transcript data for session "ses_123". Try updating OpenCode and running the command again.` |
| Session does not exist | `OpenCode session "ses_missing" was not found. Check the session ID and try again.` |

OpenCode stderr can contain progress output, internal diagnostics, terminal escapes, or sensitive values. Arbitrary stderr is not copied into the terminal error. Only a line beginning with `Error:` is eligible for display. That line is stripped of terminal control sequences, passed through Entire’s redaction, collapsed to one line, and limited to 300 runes. If OpenCode exits without a structured error line, attach reports:

```text
OpenCode could not export session "ses_123".
```

When agent auto-detection also fails, that secondary failure stays in debug logs instead of adding the noisy `(also tried auto-detecting other agents: ...)` suffix. Auto-detection also skips the agent that was resolved from existing session state, rather than relying only on the CLI flag.

## Compatibility

Agents without `TranscriptFetcher` keep their existing explicit-session-ID behavior. A valid fallback transcript still wins after a fetch failure, and cancellation remains distinguishable through error unwrapping.

This PR does not include cache staging, cache-preservation changes, full transcript-shape validation, OpenCode session enumeration, the attach picker, or historical import. Cache integrity and bounded subprocess capture can be reviewed separately without blocking this error-reporting fix.

## Merge order

The preferred path is to include this follow-up in #1877 before that PR merges, so the new fetch capability lands with its user-facing failure handling.

If the changes remain in separate PRs, #1877 must merge first. This draft targets `main` from the start, so no base change is needed afterward. Once #1877 is on `main`, GitHub will remove its shared commit from this PR’s diff.

## Testing

The regression was reproduced on #1877 before the fix: a failed fetch followed by no fallback lost the fetch cause and returned the generic transcript-not-found error.

Focused tests cover fetch failure retention, successful fallback, agents without `TranscriptFetcher`, missing executables, timeouts, permission failures, useful and unstructured stderr, invalid JSON, and failed secondary auto-detection.

`mise run check` passed. This includes formatting, lint with zero issues, race-enabled unit and integration tests, all 59 deterministic Vogon scenarios, and all 4 Roger scenarios.

The current binary was also exercised with real OpenCode inside an isolated temporary Git repository. A nonexistent session produced:

```text
OpenCode could not export session "ses_nonexistent_ux_test": Unexpected error
```

### 1969 fix: dedupe files_touched at the checkpoint write boundary
this is the dedupe half of #1937, split into its own pr after @Soph asked to keep the gitrepo fix separate ([comment](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1937#issuecomment-5267402995)). the underlying report is entireio/cli#1927: a single checkpoint `metadata.json` grew to 111.79 MB, 94% of it `files_touched`, holding 1,292,257 entries of which only 67,340 were unique — a 19x duplication factor. once that blob crossed github's 100 MB limit, `entire/checkpoints/v1` became permanently unpushable, and the failure only surfaced as a warning tacked onto unrelated pushes.

## what this does

`writeSessionToSubdirectory` used to write `opts.FilesTouched` into the session metadata exactly as handed to it. it now runs the list through `NormalizeFilesTouched` first: dedupe, sort, normalize to forward slashes. on the issue's measured numbers that alone takes the blob from 111.79 MB to about 5.5 MB and back under the limit.

a few details that came out of review on #1937 (thanks @ecgang):

* the helper preserves nil-versus-empty. `files_touched` is marshaled without `omitempty`, so nil stays JSON `null` and a non-nil empty list stays `[]` — the wire format is unchanged for empty inputs.
* both live backends inherit the fix through the shared `treeWriter` (`gitRefsStore` embeds it), and the test now runs against both the git-branch and git-refs stores instead of leaning on the embedding argument.
* the fsstore reference backend applies the same normalization, since it's the worked example the next real backend would copy.

## why it warns instead of deduping silently

soph's worry on #1937 was that a silent dedupe hides the actual bug, and it's a fair worry: every merge path in the current code already dedupes — i audited them, and @ecgang audited them independently and came up equally empty (their comment on #1927 lists the paths) — so whatever produced the 19x duplication is either a version older than 0.8.42 or a path nobody has found yet. so when the boundary strips duplicates, it now logs a warning with the session id and the reported-versus-unique counts. if a live producer exists, it shows up in `.entire/logs` instead of disappearing into the dedupe.

## tests

* `TestWriteCommitted_DeduplicatesFilesTouched`: duplicated input written, permanent record read back deduplicated and sorted, against both git backends. fails without the boundary dedupe.
* empty-input cases pin the nil-versus-`[]` behavior.
* `mise run check` green: fmt, lint, unit, integration, and the e2e canary.

## what this does not do

it can't repair a branch that already carries an oversized blob — git history is immutable, so an affected `entire/checkpoints/v1` needs a one-time rewrite, as discussed on the issue. and it deliberately doesn't touch the nested-checkout walking, which is the other (unbounded) half of the issue and lives in #1937.

### 1937 fix: stop checkpoint metadata.json outgrowing github's blob limit
fixes entireio/cli#1927 (fixes 1 and 2 from the issue; 3 and 4 discussed there as follow-ups).

## what this does

on repos with nested git checkouts under the repo root (agent worktrees, linked worktrees, vendored clones), a session's `files_touched` grew without bound until one checkpoint `metadata.json` blob crossed github's 100 MB limit and `entire/checkpoints/v1` became permanently unpushable. two independent defects compounded (measured in the issue: 1,292,257 entries, 67,340 unique, 96% of them inside other checkouts).

**1.** `fix(gitrepo)`**: exclude nested git checkouts from worktree status.**<br>real git treats a directory containing a `.git` entry as a repository boundary (`dir.c`) and never descends into it. go-git's status walk only skips entries *named* `.git` (`utils/merkletrie/filesystem/node.go`) and never checks whether a directory *contains* one, so it descends into every nested checkout and reports all its files as untracked. `gitrepo.Status`, already the enforced choke point for status reads, now drops untracked entries whose ancestor directory contains a `.git` entry (directory or worktree-style file; one memoized `Lstat` per unique ancestor). tracked entries are kept wherever they sit, matching git. this was the unbounded half: every new agent worktree multiplied the recorded set.

the walk cost itself (go-git still descends before the filter runs) is a go-git gap. i plan to raise an issue upstream, and likely a pr: the git-faithful fix is a boundary check in go-git's filesystem noder, which would benefit every go-git consumer.

**2.** `fix(checkpoint)`**: dedupe** `files_touched` **at the write boundary.**<br>every merge path already deduplicates (checked on v0.8.42 too), yet the reporter's blob proves duplicated paths reach the permanent record through some path that bypasses the merge helpers. instead of only hunting that producer, the session-metadata write in `writeSessionToSubdirectory` now passes `FilesTouched` through the existing `mergeFilesTouched` helper (dedupe, sort, slash-normalize), so no producer, past or future, can write duplicates into the immutable record. on the issue's numbers this alone shrinks the blob from 111.79 MB to roughly 5.5 MB. covers both git-backed stores (branch and refs) via the shared `treeWriter`; the fs store is test-only.

## why this shape

* the issue asked which form the nested-checkout skip should take: skip-any-dir-containing-`.git` vs `git worktree list`. this pr uses the former, since agent worktrees are not always worktrees *of the host repo*; a foreign clone under the repo root would slip past `git worktree list`.
* filtering at the `gitrepo.Status` choke point (rather than per consumer) fixes `DetectFileChanges`, attribution, and carry-forward at once, and the forbidigo rule already guarantees no caller can bypass it.
* untracked-only filtering matches git: index entries are always reported, even inside a directory that later grew a `.git`.

* `TestStatus_SkipsNestedCheckouts` (gitrepo): nested clone with `.git` directory, linked worktree with `.git` file, depth > 1, own untracked files kept, tracked file inside a nested checkout kept as modified. fails without the filter.
